final_recommendation: The room converged on a bilateral U.S.-Mexico protocol amendment to strengthen labor enforcement, with Mexico signing by Sunday night and Congress filing Monday morning. The amendment adds automatic tariff snapback (30 days post-monitor report, zero presidential discretion), independent trilateral monitors with unannounced factory access, and union notification within 48 hours—framed publicly as a 'fix' that locks enforcement rather than reopening the deal.
minority_objections: Canada insisted any amendment remain strictly bilateral U.S.-Mexico and not touch trilateral text, dairy, or Chapter 19—threatening to walk if the amendment process widened scope
Mexico demanded sovereignty-protecting language: trilateral panel structure with monitors reporting to the panel first (not direct U.S. inspectors), then notifying unions within 48 hours
key_conflicts: Administration delay vs. Congress/labor 5 PM deadline for automatic snapback text—administration failed to commit, triggering amendment path
Labor's demand for 'direct union reporting' vs. Mexico's insistence on trilateral panel structure to avoid U.S. inspectors on Mexican soil
Business lobby pressure for immediate ratification vs. labor/Congress refusal to ratify without enforceable teeth
Timing tension: Congress filing amendment Monday vs. Mexico needing to sign protocol by Sunday night to prevent full deal reopening
key_concessions: Mexico accepted independent trilateral monitors with unannounced factory access and automatic tariff snapback—major sovereignty concession framed as 'enforcement without occupation'
Labor accepted trilateral panel reporting structure (monitors report to panel, panel notifies unions within 48 hours) instead of direct union reporting
Congress agreed to frame amendment as 'enforcement fix' rather than 'deal failure' to preserve ratification momentum
Canada accepted bilateral amendment path as long as trilateral text remained untouched
red_lines: Labor: no ratification without automatic snapback and zero presidential discretion—'toothless enforcement' blocks floor vote
Mexico: no U.S. labor inspectors on Mexican soil—only independent trilateral monitors acceptable
Canada: no reopening of dairy concessions or Chapter 19 dispute settlement—bilateral amendment only or Canada walks
Congress: administration must commit to enforcement text by 5 PM or amendment files Monday—no further delays
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Administration's actual willingness/capacity to commit to automatic snapback language—room assumed USTR delay was political cover, not genuine legal constraint
Risk that 'amendment as fix' media frame fails and public/Congress perceives reopening as deal instability
Potential for Mexico's Congress to reject protocol if domestic opposition frames trilateral monitors as sovereignty infringement
Timeline risk: Mexico signing Sunday night, Congress filing Monday morning leaves zero buffer for text disputes or last-minute changes
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Mexico's signature actually lands by Sunday 10 PM deadline with final monitor-reporting language locked
Whether business lobby mobilization (Chamber, Roundtable, NAM) can actually flip enough House votes by Friday floor vote
Whether media narrative holds as 'enforcement fix' vs. 'deal stalled/reopened' through Monday-Friday news cycle
Whether Canada's ratification proceeds immediately after Mexico signs or if domestic review delays surface
Whether automatic snapback language survives legal/political review once formalized in amendment text
uncertainty_notes: The room landed on a high-risk, high-speed path: Mexico signs protocol by Sunday night with trilateral panel structure, Congress files bilateral amendment Monday framed as 'enforcement fix,' business mobilizes votes for Friday floor ratification. Success depends on: (1) Mexico's signature landing on time with monitor-reporting language locked, (2) media frame holding as 'fix' not 'failure,' (3) business lobby flipping enough votes in 4 days, (4) no last-minute text disputes derailing timeline. The administration's failure to commit by 5 PM forced amendment path—whether that was political calculation or genuine constraint remains unresolved.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Dominated every round—Congress stated 'votes aren't there as written,' labor threatened floor blockade, 5 PM deadline failure triggered amendment path, entire room structured around ratification being contingent on enforcement fix
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Central driver—labor demanded automatic snapback/zero discretion, threatened public opposition, set 5 PM ultimatum, refused to endorse without written guarantees, shaped final protocol language on monitors and union reporting
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Genuinely developed—business committed to mobilize Chamber/Roundtable/NAM for floor votes contingent on enforcement text landing, pressured administration on timeline, but not the dominant thread (labor/Congress drove harder)
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Real consideration throughout—Canada repeatedly insisted bilateral-only amendment to protect dairy/Chapter 19, threatened to walk if trilateral text reopened, but defensive posture rather than driving force
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Genuinely discussed—Mexico drew hard line against U.S. inspectors, negotiated trilateral panel structure, insisted on government staying in enforcement chain, but accepted monitors/snapback as compromise
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Real consideration—media actor framed narratives ('fix' vs. 'stalled'), Congress/labor used public pressure as leverage, but tactical tool rather than dominant driver of room's direction
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Central theme—room treated ratification as contingent on amendment, framed protocol as necessary to prevent deal collapse, structured timeline around bilateral fix preserving trilateral text, stability depended on enforcement compromise
